title: Cisco discloses second actively exploited zero-day in a week, with maximum severity score
excerpt: The new flaw, CVE-2026-76460, lets unauthenticated attackers bypass Cisco's Identity Services Engine to gain root access — days after a separate critical zero-day in Cisco's email gateways came under attack.
body:
• Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-76460 on Wednesday: an authentication-bypass flaw in Identity Services Engine (ISE) and ISE Passive Identity Connector, rated CVSS 10.0 and under active exploitation.
  • No credentials or user interaction are required; a crafted request to an API endpoint can bypass the web management interface and yield command execution with root privileges.
  • Fixes ship in ISE and ISE-PIC 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4; no workaround exists, though access-control lists can temporarily restrict management traffic.
  • The warning follows CVE-2026-76461 — a separate 9.8-rated zero-day in Cisco's Secure Email Gateway disclosed days earlier that is also being actively exploited.

Enterprise network administrators are facing a second emergency patch cycle in as many weeks after Cisco disclosed on Wednesday that a critical zero-day vulnerability in its Identity Services Engine (ISE) is being actively exploited in the wild.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76460, carries the maximum CVSS severity score of 10.0. According to Cisco's advisory, insufficient authentication controls on an API within ISE allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass the product's web-based management interface entirely — no credentials, no user interaction — and potentially gain command execution with root privileges.

The bug that bypasses authentication

ISE is Cisco's network access control platform: the software that decides which devices and users are allowed onto a corporate network. Cisco says the vulnerability lies in an API endpoint whose authentication controls were insufficient, letting an attacker send a crafted request straight past the management login. Vulnerable versions of ISE and ISE Passive Identity Connector (ISE-PIC) are affected regardless of configuration, Cisco said — default settings offer no protection.

The company warned that root-level access could let attackers remove or conceal traces of an intrusion, complicating any forensic effort to determine whether an appliance had been breached. Cisco discovered the flaw while resolving a Technical Assistance Center support case and has not said who is exploiting it, how long the attacks have been underway, or what intruders have done after gaining access. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

A separate zero-day in Cisco's email gateways

Wednesday's disclosure arrives days after Cisco confirmed active exploitation of a different critical flaw: CVE-2026-76461, affecting its Secure Email Gateway and Secure Email and Web Manager appliances. That vulnerability — rated 9.8 — lies in the email-parsing logic of Cisco's AsyncOS software. An unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted email containing malicious SQL statements through an affected gateway and, if the exploit works, escalate to command execution with root privileges on the underlying operating system. The intended recipient does not need to open the message for the gateway to be compromised.

Cisco disclosed that bug on September 14 after its Product Security Incident Response Team (PSIRT) became aware of exploitation; CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day and set a September 17 remediation deadline for federal civilian agencies. Fixed AsyncOS releases are 15.5.5-014, 16.0.4-302 and 16.5.0-780, and Cisco said there are no workarounds. Cisco's Secure Email Cloud devices were investigated and upgraded to AsyncOS 16.5.0-780, the company said.

"A root shell from a crafted email is about as bad as it gets, and the CVSS score almost undersells it."

— Gunter Ollmann, chief technology officer at Cobalt, speaking to Security Point Break

Ollmann added that defenders should worry less about the exploit itself than about what comes after: "Cisco is telling people attackers can wipe their own indicators of compromise once they have root. If your detection strategy leans on matching known IoCs after the fact, you may have already missed the intrusion."

What Cisco is telling admins to do

Cisco urged customers to install the ISE fixes immediately. Admins should review ISE access logs for suspicious usernames on every node in a distributed deployment, and check network and firewall logs held outside the affected device for signs of unexpected uploads or downloads. If evidence of possible exploitation turns up, Cisco "strongly recommends" reimaging affected nodes and restoring configurations from backup if necessary.

No workaround exists, although Cisco said infrastructure access-control lists can serve as a temporary mitigation to restrict management and control-plane traffic reaching affected systems. Customers on ISE 3.0, which has reached the end of software maintenance, must migrate to a supported release.

Why this matters for Indian IT teams

India's technology workforce sits squarely in the blast radius of both flaws. Indian engineers and managed-security teams run the network operations centers and security operations centers of enterprises across the U.S., Europe and the Gulf — they are the people actually patching ISE deployments and sifting email-gateway logs this week. For them, the risk is not abstract: ISE governs who gets onto the corporate network, so a bypass of its authentication is a bypass of the front door.

What's next

September is shaping up as a patching gauntlet. The Register reports that Wednesday's advisory accompanied a batch of other ISE vulnerabilities, including two more advisories carrying maximum 10.0 CVSS scores and a trio of remote-code-execution flaws scoring up to 9.9. Admins should treat this as a multi-week remediation effort rather than a single patch — and, given Cisco's own warnings about log tampering, assume that the absence of evidence in local logs is not evidence of safety.
image_caption: A man reacts with alarm while looking at a laptop screen. Cisco disclosed two actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities this week, including a maximum-severity authentication bypass in its Identity Services Engine.
nri_angle: Indian IT professionals and managed-security teams — who run many of the world's enterprise networks and SOCs — are on the front line of this patching sprint, since ISE governs network access for the companies they support.
author: Diaspora Desk
